query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the nozzle-to-substrate distance to ~300 mm in the HVAF-i7 process will significantly increase the deposition thickness of FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy bond coats relative to the baseline achieved with a 15–45 μm feedstock at longer distances.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a particle size range of 15–45 μm, producing acceptable quality but insufficient thickness using the standard HVAF-i7 setup.
generation.intervention: Decrease the spray distance (nozzle-to-substrate distance) to approximately 300 mm.
generation.conditions: Deposition carried out using the HVAF-i7 torch under ambient conditions with similar gas composition and feedstock properties as the baseline; application on substrates with internal diameters as small as 120 mm.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle velocity leading to improved in-flight melting and splat formation, resulting in a denser, thicker coating with minimal oxidation.
generation.mechanism: A lower stand-off distance decreases the in-flight time, thereby increasing the kinetic energy of the particles and reducing their exposure to oxygen. This results in reduced oxidation and better adhesion upon impact, promoting a thicker deposit.
generation.predicted_outcome: An expected increase in coating thickness by roughly 30–50% relative to the baseline, while maintaining coating integrity and low oxidation levels.
generation.baseline: Current HVAF-i7 deposition using standard spray distances yields acceptable quality but inadequate thickness compared to the HVAF-M3 benchmark.
generation.boundary: Effective as long as the reduced distance does not induce substrate overheating or local melting, and particle oxidation remains controlled.
generation.uncertainty: Exact thickness gains and the potential for localized overheating need to be verified; the trade-off between increased kinetic energy and oxidation levels might vary with slight process changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled deposition test series on identical substrates using the HVAF-i7 system at nozzle-to-substrate distances of 300 mm versus the baseline distance. Maintain all other parameters constant.
measurements: Measure the coating thickness using cross-sectional microscopy.
Assess in-flight particle velocity via diagnostic techniques.
Quantify oxidation levels (e.g., via EDS) and adhesion quality.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If reducing the spray distance to 300 mm does not result in a statistically significant (≥30%) increase in coating thickness or causes unacceptable levels of oxidation or adhesion degradation, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. Oxidation and Phase Transformations in the Powder during HVOF Spraying
cited_evidence.text: As seen from Figure 4b, the higher oxide content in the coating deposited from a higher distance does not result in a higher microhardness. On the contrary, with an increase in the spaying distance from 150 mm to 250 mm, the microhardness decreases from 750 HV to 550 HV. Taking into account earlier observations, a noticeable decrease in the microhardness with an increase in the spraying distance can be explained by the increased porosity, the increase in the amount of the soft FCC phase, and the softening of the BCC solid solution due to Al outflow []. Thus, particle oxidation during high-temperature spraying in an oxygen-containing atmosphere considerably influences the coating properties.

MCrAlY BCs, usually deposited by high velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF), improve the adhesion of the TBC through a rough surface and compensates the misfit between the coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) of the TBC and the substrate. While exposed to high temperatures, MCrAlY coatings form a thermally grown oxide layer (TGO) on their surface. This continuously growing layer strongly affects the TBC adhesion, which depends on the TGO’s phase composition. However, a stable TGO made of α-Al2O3 is mandatory to prevent further materials oxidation and thus to protect the substrate. This may, inter alia, include barrier function to oxygen ions [,,]. Due to the number and the interaction of these complex diffusion-controlled phenomena, research projects still deal with the understanding of TBC systems oxidation behavior and its failure mechanisms [,,]. Since TBC systems have proven to be reliable in the industry as long-term protection, they continue to be used mainly in the first gas turbine blade stages, where ambient temperatures exceed 1000 °C. papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder for thermal spray (HVOF) coatings
papers.approach: The study deposited HEA coatings at varying spray distances to investigate how particle temperature, kinetic energy, and in‐flight oxidation affected coating properties (thickness, porosity, phase transformations).
papers.findings: Increasing the spray distance led to a slight decrease in coating thickness and increased porosity together with a higher oxide content due to increased particle oxidation; conversely, reducing the spray distance (thus increasing particle velocity) improved deposition efficiency.
papers.mechanism: Higher particle kinetic energy (via a reduced in-flight time / shorter spray distance) minimizes oxidation and enhances the momentum upon impact, promoting more effective melting, spreading, and adhesion – which results in thicker, denser coatings.

papers.title: Comparative Study on the Thermal Performance of Cr-CrₓOᵧ and YSZ-CoNiCrAlY Coatings Exposed at 900 °C.
papers.system: Conventional MCrAlY bond coats (including NiCoCrAlY systems) deposited by HVAF
papers.approach: Experimental evaluation of deposition parameters in thermal spray systems—specifically assessing the effect of particle velocity and nozzle-to-substrate distance on the deposition efficiency and ultimately the bond coat quality.
papers.findings: A slight gain in deposition efficiency was observed when the spray was conducted at higher particle velocities with nozzle-specific optimal distances of about 300–350 mm, leading to improved coating adhesion and ultimately better performance during high-temperature exposure.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced particle velocity results in higher in-flight momentum, reducing oxidation and improving in-flight melting and splat formation. This not only increases the effective deposition per pass (hence achieving greater thickness) but also promotes superior metallurgical bonding with the substrate.

established: For thermal spray deposition of high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings, feedstock particle size in the 15–45 μm range produces high-quality coatings in the HVAF-M3 system.
Higher particle velocities during deposition are correlated with improved melting, reduced oxidation, and enhanced deposition efficiency.

approaches_tried.approach: Optimization of spray distance (nozzle-specific distances of 300–350 mm) to achieve higher particle velocities in conventional MCrAlY bond coat deposition.
approaches_tried.outcome: A slight gain in deposition efficiency was achieved, resulting in improved coating adhesion and marginal increases in thickness.

approaches_tried.approach: Variation of spray distance in HVOF deposition (as observed for FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 based coatings) to study the influence of oxidation and kinetic energy on coating build-up.
approaches_tried.outcome: Longer spray distances decreased coating thickness due to reduced particle kinetic energy and increased oxidation, highlighting the need to control particle velocity.

mechanisms: Increased particle velocity enhances the kinetic energy of feedstock particles, leading to more effective in-flight melting and better splat formation upon impact.
Higher kinetic energy minimizes in-flight oxidation by reducing the time available for oxidation reactions, thereby resulting in denser and thicker coatings.
disagreements: There is some divergence on whether the marginal gains from increasing particle velocity offset the risks of increased oxidation if the spray distance is not precisely controlled.
The optimal balance between feedstock size, spray distance, and particle velocity remains under debate, as different systems (HVAF-M3 vs. HVAF-i7) may respond differently.
open_questions: Can the HVAF-i7 system achieve deposition thickness comparable to HVAF-M3 solely by optimizing particle velocity (via spray distance adjustments), or are other parameters (e.g., feedstock size distribution, torch power input) also critical?
What is the long-term effect of the modified deposition parameters on the structural integrity and oxidation resistance of the bond coat during high-temperature thermal-barrier service?
How does the interplay between reduced spray distance (increased kinetic energy) and potential localized overheating affect the phase stability and adhesion of the coatings?
opportunities: Investigate combining optimized spray distances (to increase particle velocity) specifically in the HVAF-i7 system with slight adjustments in feedstock size distribution to compensate for inherent system differences.

Conduct controlled experiments that vary only the nozzle-to-substrate distance in the HVAF-i7 torch under constant feedstock conditions to isolate the effect of particle velocity on coating thickness.
Explore the effects of tailored atmospheric conditions or supplemental gas flows to further reduce in-flight oxidation when increasing particle velocity.

Evaluate deposition and post-deposition mechanical performance and oxidation behavior under service-simulated thermal-cycling conditions within small internal diameters (e.g., 120 mm) to mimic actual application environments.

directions.direction: Reduce the nozzle-to-substrate distance in the HVAF-i7 spray process to increase the particle kinetic energy.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the inadequate thickness by increasing particle velocity, as evidenced by conventional MCrAlY work showing optimal spray distances around 300–350 mm (e.g., PMC8541463::web::003::1_introduction). The mechanism is well established in decreasing in‐flight oxidation and promoting better splat formation. It respects the feedstock size and coating quality constraints and appears highly feasible.

directions.direction: Increase the torch power/fuel flow rate to boost particle kinetic energy.
directions.assessment: Enhancing the energy input may increase the momentum of the particles and thus overcome thickness limitations. However, extra power could induce unwanted oxidation or overheating. While the physics of improved particle melting is known (PMC10820071::web::010::3_2_oxidation_and_phase_transformations_), careful tuning is necessary to avoid trade‐offs.

directions.direction: Preheat the substrate prior to deposition to improve splat flattening and metallurgical bonding.
directions.assessment: Substrate preheating can reduce thermal gradients upon impact and promote denser splat formation. This can increase deposition efficiency even if the particle velocity remains constant. Although not as directly linked to thickness increase as particle velocity adjustments, it complements deposition quality without altering feedstock properties. The concept finds indirect support in thermal spray adhesion studies.

directions.direction: Implement localized inert gas shrouding around the spray plume to reduce in-flight oxidation.
directions.assessment: By surrounding the spray stream with an inert gas (e.g., argon), the oxidation during flight can be minimized even when particles are accelerated for greater kinetic energy. This intervention targets both oxidation control and improved deposition efficiency, which supports thicker coatings. Feasibility depends on integrating a shrouding system with the HVAF-i7, and the underlying mechanism is consistent with oxidation‐minimizing strategies reported in the literature.

directions.direction: Modify the feedstock surface by applying a temporary anti-oxidation coating on the powder.
directions.assessment: Tailoring the powder surface could reduce premature oxidation during flight. However, this method entails modifying powder chemistry and may conflict with the constraint of using the same composition. The underlying physics is plausible but less directly tied to the deposition thickness limitation than process parameter adjustments.

candidates.hypothesis: Increasing the torch power (and hence fuel flow) by approximately 20% in the HVAF-i7 process will enhance the particle kinetic energy, leading to a thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coat deposition relative to the standard power setting.
candidates.intervention: Increase the torch power/fuel flow by about 20% while keeping the spray distance at the standard value.

candidates.hypothesis: Preheating the substrate to approximately 200 °C prior to HVAF-i7 deposition will enhance splat formation and bonding, resulting in a thicker and more adherent FeCoNiCrAl bond coat compared to deposition on room temperature substrates.
candidates.intervention: Implement a substrate preheating step, elevating the substrate temperature to around 200 °C prior to and during deposition.

candidates.hypothesis: Deploying a localized inert gas shrouding system during HVAF-i7 deposition will reduce in-flight oxidation of FeCoNiCrAl particles, allowing increased particle velocity (via reduced spray distance) to translate into a thicker, high-quality bond coat compared to unshielded deposition.
candidates.intervention: Integrate an inert gas (e.g., argon) shrouding system around the spray plume during deposition while operating at a reduced spray distance (around 300 mm).

minor_issues: The proposal does not cite any direct prior data tying torch power increases to the stated 20–40% thickness improvement, so it is partially extrapolating from general thermal spray principles.
Possible risk of excessive oxidation or detrimental microstructural changes from higher spray temperatures is acknowledged but not quantitatively addressed.
fixes: Provide or reference existing HVAF documentation or studies that demonstrate coating thickness improvements from modest increases in torch power.
Define safe operational windows for the 20% power increase (e.g., maximum allowable temperature and pressure levels) to preempt oxidation or particle overheat issues.
